raw_text:
Great. Here’s a structured 12-week upper-body focused program tailored for a 29-year-old recreational climber with a right subacromial impingement, cleared for pain-free range, no overhead loading. It emphasizes scapular stability, rotator cuff health, controlled resisted pulling/pushing with emphasis on avoiding impingement mechanics, and graded loading to support climbing performance. It also includes weekly progression, session-by-session plans, and basic recovery/nutrition guidance. All movements should be pain-free within your client’s available ROM; avoid any painful ranges or exercises that provoke impingement.

Key principles
- Pain-free ROM: Only use ranges and loads tolerable in the pain-free window. Stop if pain worsens beyond a mild, non-persistent discomfort.
- Progressive exposure: Start light, emphasize technique, scapular control, and rotator cuff engagement; gradually increase load/volume.
- Climbing specificity: Integrate anti-rotation/core, pulling strength, grip endurance, and scapular mechanics to support climbing moves without overhead loading.
- Symmetry and balance: Prioritize balanced development between left and right, given unilateral impingement risk.
- Recovery: Prioritize sleep, nutrition with adequate protein, and mobility work to reduce stiffness and improve shoulder mechanics.

Program structure
- Duration: 12 weeks
- Frequency: 3 upper-body focused sessions per week (non-consecutive days; Example: Mon/Wed/Sat)
- Split: Each week includes 3 upper-body sessions with a rotational emphasis on strength, endurance, and mobility; optional accessory climber-specific work
- Mobility: Daily 5–10 minutes focused on thoracic mobility, scapular control, and posterior chain
- Conditioning: Minimal high-impact cycling or cardio to avoid irritation; tolerance-based cardio optional

Weeks 1–4: Foundation and motor control
Goal: establish pain-free range, scapular stability, and rotator cuff engagement; build base pulling strength without overhead loading.

Sessions: 3 per week (A, B, C). Alternate A/B/C across weeks with similar structure but slightly varied loads.

Common warm-up before each session (8–12 minutes)
- Face pulls with light band: 2 sets x 15–20 reps
- Scapular push-ups or wall slides: 2 sets x 12 reps
- External rotation with resistance band at 0–20 degrees (standing or supported): 2 sets x 12 reps
- Cat-cow thoracic mobility: 1–2 minutes
- Light row pattern on a cable machine or resistance bands: 2 sets x 12 reps per side

Session A (horizontal pulling emphasis, no overhead loading)
- Seated cable row or standing T-bar row: 3 sets x 10–12 reps, load light-moderate
- Dumbbell floor press (neutral grip) or machine chest press: 3 x 10–12
- Superman with scapular retraction hold: 3 x 12
- Prone Y, T, I exercises with light dumbbells or bands: 2–3 x 12 each
- Pallof press or anti-rotation with cable: 3 x 10–12 per side
- Farmer’s carry with moderate weight (thumbs in) to build grip and shoulder stability: 2 x 30–40 seconds

Session B (pulling with isometrics and rotator cuff emphasis)
- Assisted band pull-aparts or lying horizontal rope row: 3 x 15
- Dumbbell external rotation at 0–15 degrees abduction: 3 x 12 per side
- 45° incline-sleeper press with light weight (to reduce impingement risk): 3 x 10
- Lat pulldown underhand grip to chest height (avoid full overhead range): 3 x 12
- Prone pinch or grip work: 2 x 20–30 seconds
- Stability work: single-arm anti-rotational carries with a light plate or kettlebell: 2 x 30 seconds per side

Session C (mobility + symmetry + conditioning)
- Medicine ball slams (light) or dumbbell punch-throughs (to scapular plane) 3 x 12
- Cable face pull with external rotation at 90 degrees: 3 x 12
- Dumbbell floor press or machine chest press: 3 x 12
- Isometric scapular retraction hold: 3 x 20–30 seconds
- Band-resisted dead hang scapular depression (gentle): 2 x 20–30 seconds
- Core work: dead bug or pallof variations 3 x 10–12 per side

Progression week-to-week (Weeks 1–4)
- Increase total volume by 5–10% every week if pain-free
- Maintain technique; ensure scapular depression/detraction sequences are controlled
- Keep tempo moderate (2 seconds eccentric, 1 second concentric) for most lifts
- Weekly check-in: note shoulder comfort during climbing, any overhead tasks, and any day-of-pain changes

Weeks 5–8: Strength development with controlled overhead reintroduction
Goal: progressively reintroduce light overhead loading with strict form and scapular control; increase pulling strength and shoulder stability.

Sessions: 3 per week; continue A/B/C structure with increased intensity.

Session A (horizontal push/pull emphasis)
- Barbell or dumbbell bench press (neutral grip) with controlled tempo: 4 x 8–10
- Seated cable row or chest-supported row: 4 x 8–10
- Face pulls with moderate load: 3 x 12–15
- Dumbbell floor press: 3 x 10–12
- Prone scapular Y/T/I with light resistance: 3 x 12 each
- Farmers carry: 3 x 40–60 seconds

Session B (rotator cuff strength + light overhead integration)
- Overhead press with neutral grip or landmine press at low height (if pain-free and within tolerance): 3–4 x 6–8
- Lat pulldown or assisted pull-up (avoid full overhead to start): 3–4 x 8–10
- External rotation at 0–20 degrees: 3 x 12
- Incline dumbbell press: 3 x 8–10
- Pallof press: 3 x 10–12 per side
- Core stability: 3 x 20–30 seconds anti-extension/plank variations

Session C (climber-specific grip + endurance)
- Rope/cord-assisted rows or high rep cable rows: 3–4 x 12–15
- Push-up progression (on knees or elevated) to ensure scapular control: 3 x 12–15
- Cable external rotation at 0–20 degrees: 3 x 12
- Single-arm carry variations: 2–3 x 40–60 seconds per side
- Operator mobility: thoracic extension on a foam roller 2–3 minutes total

Progression Weeks 5–8
- Overhead load: progress load by 5–10% if pain-free; keep repetitions in 6–8 or 8–10 ranges
- Increase pulling volume with 1–2 extra sets on main pulls
- Maintain scapular control cues; avoid superior glide into impingement zone

Weeks 9–12: Peak strength and climbing-specific integration
Goal: maximize upper-body strength with a focus on scapular mechanics and grip endurance; prepare for climbing demands while maintaining pain-free operation.

Sessions: 3 per week; A/B/C as structure but with higher intensity and lower reps.

Session A (horizontal press/pull + stability)
- Barbell or dumbbell bench press: 4–5 x 5–6
- Seated row (machine or cable): 4–5 x 6–8
- Face pulls: 3 x 12–15
- Floor press or incline press: 3 x 6–8
- Scapular push-ups or stability ball row: 3 x 12–15
- Farmer’s carry or suitcase carry: 3 x 45–60 seconds

Session B (controlled overhead loading under supervision)
- Dumbbell or landmine press from chest height: 4 x 6–8
- Lat pulldown with controlled tempo: 4 x 6–8
- External rotation with light to moderate load: 3 x 12
- Cable pullover or high-to-low rows: 3 x 8–12
- Pallof press: 3 x 12 per side
- Core: anti-rotation or suitcase carry: 3 x 30–40 seconds per side

Session C (climbing-specific endurance and grip)
- High-rep inverted rows or ring rows: 3–4 x 10–12
- Push-up variations with scapular control: 4 x 12–15
- Band-resisted pull-aparts or cable face pulls: 3 x 15–20
- Grip endurance: fat gripz or thick bar holds: 3 x 20–40 seconds
- Korean deadlift grip or farmer carries: 3 x 40–60 seconds
- Mobility: 5–10 minutes focusing on thoracic mobility and posterior shoulder

Deload week (Week 12 end or last week as needed)
- Reduce volume by 40–50% and intensity by 10–20%
- Foam roll, mobility work, and light technique-only sessions
- Monitor symptoms; ensure full pain-free function before returning to climbing intensity

Rehabilitation and mechanics notes
- Internal/external rotation balance: Ensure external rotation strength is balanced with internal rotation to prevent anterior glide and subacromial irritation.
- Scapular rhythm: Emphasize scapular upward rotation, depression, and posterior tilt during pushing/pulling to reduce impingement risk.
- Overhead loading caution: If any overhead press triggers pain, revert to floor press, landmine press at chest height, or incline press with neutral grip.
- Climbing-specific adaptation: Emphasize grip stability, scapular retraction, and core engagement during climbing moves. Include isometric holds at various angles to simulate crimp and open-handed grips without aggravating the shoulder.
- Return-to-climb criteria: Pain-free ROM, no increase in symptoms during pulling, pushing, or overhead activities. Ability to perform controlled weighted overhead movements without joint irritation.

Nutrition and recovery recommendations
- Protein intake: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day to support tissue repair and strength gains.
- Calorie balance: Maintain a modest caloric intake aligned with activity level to support recovery; avoid a sustained energy deficit during higher training weeks.
- Hydration: 2–3 liters per day, more if sweating heavily during climbs.
- Sleep: Aim for 7–9 hours per night; consider short naps if training load is high.
- Anti-inflammatory approach: Include omega-3 fats (1–2 g/day) if tolerated, turmeric/curcumin as recommended by clinician, and ensure adequate micronutrients (calcium, vitamin D, magnesium) to support tendon health.
- Mobility and recovery: 5–10 minutes daily of thoracic mobility, scapular stabilization, and posterior chain work; consider weekly soft-tissue work (myofascial release) if tolerated.

Climbing-specific integration
- Weekly climbing days: 2–3 sessions per week, separated from heavy lifting by at least 4–6 hours if possible.
- Climbing exercises: Focus on routes requiring crimps, slopers, and edges but avoid high-overhead loads during the initial 4 weeks. Gradually incorporate gym climbing with controlled, pain-free loads.
- Pre- and post-climb: 5–10 minutes of scapular activation and rotator cuff stabilization, plus gentle shoulder mobility.

Monitoring and adjustments
- Pain scale: 0–2 during activity, 0 at rest; stop or modify if pain exceeds 2–3 or lasts >24 hours.
- Climb-specific symptoms: Note any local tenderness around the subacromial area, or pain during overhead reach, or pulling movements.
- ROM checks: Weekly checks of pain-free ROM; if ROM reduces or pain increases, adjust volume and avoid overhead workloads until comfortable.

If you’d like, I can tailor this plan further to match her exact gym equipment, preferred exercises, or any constraints (time, travel, equipment like bands vs. machines). I can also provide a weekly progression table with specific load targets (in lbs/kg) based on initial strength testing or a 1RM bench/press estimation, plus a climber-specific warm-up protocol and a printable 12-week plan.
